5Area One: Your Device And The Internet (Skills 1 To 3)

Everything starts here. These three skills are the doorway to all the others.

Skill 1: Using your phone and computer confidently

What it is. Being comfortable with the device in your hand: turning it on, connecting it to the internet, installing and deleting apps, changing settings, charging it wisely and fixing common little problems.

Why it matters. If your device feels like a mystery box, every task takes twice as long and feels twice as stressful. Confidence here saves hours across a year.

What to learn.

  • How to connect to Wi-Fi and to mobile data, and how to tell which one you are using.
  • How to install an app from the official store (the App Store on an iPhone, Google Play on Android), and how to remove one.
  • How to find and change settings: screen brightness, text size, notifications, sound and language.
  • How to check your storage so your phone does not run out of space.
  • How to update your software, because updates fix security problems.
  • How to restart a frozen device. Holding the power button and restarting solves a surprising number of problems.
  • On a computer: how to open and close programs, switch between windows, use the desktop and use the search bar to find things.

Free tool. Your device's own Settings app, and the help pages on the manufacturer's website.

Practise it. Open Settings. Find your storage and write down how much is free. Delete one app you never use. Change the text size to a comfortable level. Turn off notifications for one app that interrupts you. Done.

Pro Tip 💡 If you get stuck on any device problem, search for the exact wording. For example, type "iPhone storage full how to fix" or "Android phone will not connect to Wi-Fi." Add your phone model if you know it. Someone has almost certainly solved your exact problem and explained it.

Skill 2: Typing and keyboard shortcuts

What it is. Typing at a comfortable speed and using shortcuts, which are key combinations that do a task quickly. A keyboard shortcut is simply pressing two or three keys together to do something that would otherwise take several clicks.

Why it matters. Almost every digital job involves typing. Slow, hunting-and-pecking typing drains energy. Shortcuts make you feel fast and capable.

What to learn. Start with the shortcuts you will use daily. On Windows they use the Ctrl key. On a Mac they use the Command key.

What it doesWindowsMac
CopyCtrl + CCommand + C
PasteCtrl + VCommand + V
CutCtrl + XCommand + X
UndoCtrl + ZCommand + Z
Select everythingCtrl + ACommand + A
SaveCtrl + SCommand + S
Find a word on the pageCtrl + FCommand + F
Switch between open programsAlt + TabCommand + Tab

On a phone, learn to copy and paste by pressing and holding on text, to use voice typing with the microphone symbol on your keyboard and to turn on autocorrect or turn it off if it keeps changing your words.

Free tool. Typing practice websites such as Keybr, TypingClub and Monkeytype. Check current features on each site.

Practise it. Spend ten minutes on a typing practice site. Then open a note, write five sentences about your day and practise copy, paste and undo. Aim for accuracy first. Speed follows on its own.

Coffee Break ☕ Do not chase speed. A steady thirty-five to forty words a minute with few mistakes is more than enough for most online work.

Skill 3: Browsing the internet and searching well

What it is. Using a browser (the app you use to visit websites, such as Chrome, Safari, Firefox or Edge) and knowing how to search so that you find what you need quickly.

Why it matters. The internet holds the answer to almost any practical question, but only if you know how to ask. Good searching is like having a free tutor.

What to learn.

  • The difference between the address bar (where you type a website address) and a search engine (a website like Google or Bing that finds pages for you).
  • How to open a new tab, switch tabs and close tabs you do not need.
  • How to bookmark a page so you can return to it.
  • How to read search results. The top few are often adverts, marked with a label such as "Sponsored" or "Ad." They are not necessarily bad, but they are not neutral.
  • How to search in clear phrases. Compare "money" with "how to make a simple monthly budget in a spreadsheet." The second is far better.
  • Search shortcuts: put quotation marks around an exact phrase, add a minus sign to remove a word, and add the word "free" or "for beginners" to get gentler results.
  • How to check the address of a site before trusting it, which we will return to in the scam chapters.

Free tool. Any browser, plus the search engine of your choice.

Practise it. Find the answer to this question using only search: "How do I convert a Word document to PDF on my phone?" Bookmark the page that helps most. Then write down which search words worked best.

6Area Two: Email, Files And Staying Safe (Skills 4 To 8)

This area is where beginners most often get hurt, either by losing important things or by being tricked. Take your time here. Of all 25 skills, these five protect you the most.

Skill 4: Email

What it is. Email (electronic mail) is a message you send through the internet to someone's email address. An email address has two parts joined by an @ sign, for example name@example.com. The part before the @ is the person, and the part after it is the service that holds their mailbox.

Why it matters. Email is still the main way that businesses, schools, employers and clients communicate formally. Almost every online account you will ever create needs an email address, and password resets are sent there. If you lose your email, you can lose access to everything.

What to learn.

  • How to create an account. Free services such as Gmail, Outlook and others work well. Choose a simple, professional address, ideally some version of your real name. An address like sunshinebabygirl2005 may be fun with friends but looks odd on a job application.
  • How to write a message with the four parts: the To line (who receives it), the Subject (a short summary), the body (the message) and the signature (your name at the end).
  • The difference between Reply, Reply all and Forward. Reply goes only to the sender. Reply all goes to everyone on the original message, which is rarely what you want. Forward sends the message on to someone new.
  • What Cc and Bcc mean. Cc copies someone in, openly. Bcc copies someone in secretly, so others cannot see their address.
  • How to attach a file, and how to check that the attachment really went.
  • How to use folders or labels and how to search your inbox so you can find old messages.
  • How to set up a short signature with your name and, if relevant, a link.
  • How to tell the difference between a real and a fake email, which we cover in Skill 7.

A simple formula for a clear email.

1. A subject that says what the email is about: "Question about Tuesday's meeting." 2. A greeting: "Hello Mr Okafor," or "Hi Chioma,". 3. One sentence stating why you are writing. 4. The details, kept short, with any questions numbered. 5. A polite close and your name: "Thank you, Ruth."

Free tool. Gmail, Outlook or the mail app your phone already has.

Practise it. Send an email to yourself with a subject, a short message and one attached photo. Open it, reply to it and create a folder or label called "Important" to hold it.

Pro Tip 💡 Read your email aloud once before you send an important one. You will catch missing words and sentences that sound harsher than you meant.

Skill 5: Files, folders and cloud storage

What it is. A file is one saved item, such as a photo, a document or a video. A folder holds files, like a drawer holds papers. Cloud storage means saving your files on the internet instead of only on your device, so you can reach them from anywhere. Google Drive, iCloud, OneDrive and Dropbox are examples.

Why it matters. Phones get lost, dropped and stolen. Laptops break. If your only copy of your CV, certificates or client work lives on one device, you are one accident away from losing it. Cloud storage and a tidy folder system are the cheapest insurance you will ever buy.

What to learn.

  • How to name files clearly. "Final final 2 copy" is a trap. Use a pattern such as "2026-03-CV-Ruth-Eze" or "Invoice-Adaora-March".
  • How to build a simple folder structure. For example: Personal, Work, Learning, Money. Inside Money you might have Receipts, Invoices and Budgets.
  • How to upload, download and share a file.
  • How to move, rename, copy and delete files and, importantly, how to recover something you deleted from the trash or recycle bin.
  • What a backup is: a second copy kept somewhere else. A good rule is to keep your important files in at least two places.
  • How much free storage you get. Free amounts and plans change, so check current details on the service you choose.

Free tool. Google Drive, or the storage service built into your phone.

Practise it. Create a folder called "Important Documents." Photograph or scan your ID or certificates, name them clearly and upload them. Then search for one of them by name to prove you can find it.

Common Mistake 🚨 Keeping everything on the desktop or in the Downloads folder feels convenient until it holds four hundred files and you cannot find your certificate. Spend ten minutes a week putting things where they belong.

Skill 6: Passwords and two-step verification

What it is. A password is the secret that proves an account is yours. Two-step verification (also called two-factor authentication or 2FA) adds a second proof, such as a code sent to your phone, so a stolen password is not enough.

Why it matters. Many people reuse one password everywhere. When one website is hacked, criminals try that same password on your email, your bank and your social media. That one mistake causes a huge share of account break-ins.

What to learn.

  • What makes a password strong. Length matters more than tricks. A long phrase of several unrelated words is strong and easier to remember than a short jumble of symbols.
  • Why you should never use the same password twice, especially for your email.
  • What a password manager is: an app that creates and remembers strong passwords for you, so you only need to remember one master password. Many phones and browsers have one built in, and dedicated apps exist as well. Check current features and prices before you choose.
  • How to turn on two-step verification for your email first, then your banking and social accounts.
  • Why you must never share a verification code with anyone. A real company will not ask you to read it out.
  • How to set up account recovery options, such as a backup email or phone number, and keep them up to date.

Free tool. Your phone's built-in password manager, or a trusted free password manager.

Practise it. Change the password on your main email to a long phrase you have never used before. Turn on two-step verification for it. Write the master password on paper and keep it somewhere safe at home, not on your phone.

Reality Check 👀 I will say it plainly because it matters: if someone gets into your email, they can reset the passwords on nearly everything else. Protect your email like it is the key to your house.

Skill 7: Spotting scams and phishing

What it is. A scam is a trick to take your money, information or access. Phishing is the most common kind: a fake message that pretends to be from a bank, a delivery company, an employer or a friend, and tries to make you click a link or share details. When it arrives by text message it is sometimes called smishing, and by phone call, vishing.

Why it matters. Scammers do not need to be clever. They only need you to be tired, rushed or hopeful for one moment. The best defence is not fear. It is a calm habit.

The warning signs.

  • Urgency. "Your account will be closed in 24 hours." Real organisations rarely threaten you this way.
  • Requests for secrets. No genuine bank, employer or platform will ask for your full password, your PIN or the code sent to your phone.
  • Too good to be true. "Earn a large amount daily for liking videos." Real work does not work like that.
  • Pressure to pay in unusual ways. Gift cards, crypto transfers to strangers or paying "to unlock" a prize or job.
  • A strange address. Look closely at the sender's email address and the link. Scammers swap letters, such as "paypa1" with a number one.
  • Spelling and tone that feel off. Not always, but often.
  • Messages from "friends" asking for money. Their account may have been taken over. Call them to check.

The calm routine. Whenever a message makes your heart race, do these four things:

1. Pause. Do nothing for five minutes. 2. Do not click. Do not open the link or the attachment. 3. Check another way. Open the company's real app or type the website address yourself. Or call the number printed on your card or on the official website. 4. Report and delete. Use the report button in your email or messaging app.

Free tool. The report-spam and report-phishing buttons in your email and messaging apps. Your country's consumer protection or cyber-safety agency usually publishes free scam guidance. Search for it by name.

Practise it. Look at the spam folder in your email. Choose three messages and find three warning signs in each. This trains your eye.

Big Sis Note 💖 If you ever fall for a scam, please do not feel ashamed. Clever, careful people get tricked every day. Shame keeps people quiet, and quiet helps scammers. We will cover exactly what to do later in this guide.

Skill 8: Privacy and your digital footprint

What it is. Your digital footprint is the trail of information about you online: your posts, photos, comments, tags, accounts and even the things others say about you. Privacy settings are the controls that decide who can see what.

Why it matters. Employers, clients and sometimes scammers look people up. Things you posted years ago can still be found. A little care now protects your reputation, your safety and your peace of mind.

What to learn.

  • How to check your social media privacy settings. Look for options about who can see your posts, who can message you and who can tag you.
  • How to search your own name in a search engine and see what comes up. This is called a self-search and it is smart to do every few months.
  • What location sharing is and why you should turn it off for apps that do not need it.
  • What app permissions are. Apps ask to use your camera, contacts, microphone and location. Allow only what the app truly needs.
  • How to think before you post. A useful test: "Would I be comfortable if my future boss, my grandmother and a stranger all saw this?"
  • Why you should be careful with personal details such as your home address, your full birth date, your ID numbers and your travel plans.
  • How to use public Wi-Fi carefully. Avoid banking or entering important passwords on public networks.

Free tool. The privacy settings inside each app, and your phone's permissions menu.

Practise it. Do a self-search. Open each social account you have and check the privacy settings. Review the permissions on your phone and turn off location access for three apps that do not need it.

Did You Know? 🧠 Many apps are free because your information is part of the business. That is not automatically sinister, but it is a good reason to read what an app asks for before you tap "Allow."

A short word on what these five skills buy you

Take a breath here, because this area is dense. Notice what you have just learned. You can set up and use an email address properly. You can keep your files safe and findable. You can protect your accounts. You can spot a trap. You can control what the world sees. If you did nothing else in this guide, you would already be far ahead of many people online.

7Area Three: Everyday Productivity (Skills 9 To 15)

These are the tools of ordinary working life. Employers call them "basic computer skills" and often list them in job adverts. Clients assume you have them. If you learn these seven, you will be able to produce neat, professional work.

Skill 9: Documents (word processing)

What it is. A word processor is a program for writing and formatting text: letters, CVs, reports, proposals. Microsoft Word and Google Docs are the best-known examples.

Why it matters. A clear, neat document makes you look careful and professional before anyone has read a word.

What to learn.

  • How to open, type, save and name a document.
  • Basic formatting: bold, italics, underline, font and size. Use one simple font and a readable size such as eleven or twelve point.
  • How to use headings and bullet lists to organise information.
  • How to set alignment, spacing and margins so a page looks tidy.
  • How to use spell check, and why you should still proofread, because spell check will not catch "form" when you meant "from."
  • How to insert a picture or a table.
  • How to export or download a document as a PDF so the layout does not change on someone else's device.
  • How to use Find and replace, which changes every instance of a word at once.

Free tool. Google Docs (free with a Google account) or the free web versions of other word processors. Check current features and limits.

Practise it. Write a one-page document called "About Me" with a heading, two short paragraphs and a bullet list of three skills. Download it as a PDF and email it to yourself.

Skill 10: Spreadsheets

What it is. A spreadsheet is a grid of rows and columns where you store information and do calculations. Each little box is a cell. Google Sheets and Microsoft Excel are the most common.

Why it matters. Spreadsheets are everywhere: budgets, price lists, client trackers, schedules, sales records. Even a tiny bit of spreadsheet skill makes you instantly more useful in an office or a small business.

What to learn.

  • How rows (numbered), columns (lettered) and cells (like A1, B2) work.
  • How to type, edit and format data, including making a header row bold.
  • How to do simple sums. Type an equals sign and then a formula. For example, =SUM(B2:B10) adds everything from cell B2 to B10.
  • A few useful formulas: SUM (add), AVERAGE (the middle value), COUNT (how many entries) and simple multiplication with an asterisk, such as =B2*C2.
  • How to sort a list from A to Z or smallest to largest, and how to filter to show only certain rows.
  • How to make a simple chart.
  • How to freeze the top row so headings stay visible as you scroll.

Free tool. Google Sheets. Check current features.

Practise it. Build a tiny monthly budget. Column A is the item, column B is the amount. List five items, add a total at the bottom with =SUM, then sort the items from the biggest to the smallest.

Coffee Break ☕ Do not let the word "formula" scare you. A formula is just a sentence you write to the spreadsheet: "please add these." You will use only three or four for a long time.

Skill 11: Presentations and slides

What it is. A presentation is a set of slides that you show while you talk, or that people read on their own. Google Slides, PowerPoint and Canva all make them.

Why it matters. Pitching an idea, teaching, reporting to a manager, introducing a business: all of these use slides. Clear slides help people understand you quickly.

What to learn.

  • How to add, duplicate, reorder and delete slides.
  • How to use a template so the design is done for you.
  • The golden rules: one idea per slide, few words, large text, plenty of space and high contrast between text and background.
  • How to add an image, a simple chart or a short list.
  • How to present on a screen, and how to export your slides as a PDF.

Free tool. Google Slides or Canva.

Practise it. Make a five-slide presentation called "My Goals for This Year." Slide one is the title. Slides two to four hold one goal each, with one short sentence. Slide five says what your first step is.

Skill 12: PDFs and e-signatures

What it is. A PDF (Portable Document Format) is a file that looks the same on every device, which makes it perfect for CVs, contracts, invoices and forms. An e-signature is a digital version of your signature that you add to a document on a screen.

Why it matters. Employers, clients, schools and government offices ask for PDFs constantly. A Word file can shift and break on someone else's computer. A PDF stays put.

What to learn.

  • How to turn a document into a PDF, using "Download as PDF" or "Print to PDF."
  • How to open and read a PDF on your phone and computer.
  • How to fill in a PDF form on your device.
  • How to add your signature. Many free tools let you draw, type or upload a signature. Some official situations require a special type of signature, so check what the receiving organisation accepts.
  • How to merge several PDFs into one and how to compress a large PDF so it can be emailed.
  • How to scan a paper document using your phone camera and save it as a PDF. Many phones have a scanner built in, and free scanning apps exist too.

Free tool. Your phone's built-in scanner, free online PDF tools and the PDF options inside Google Docs. Be careful with unknown websites: avoid uploading private documents, such as ID or bank statements, to sites you do not trust.

Practise it. Scan one page from a notebook with your phone. Save it as a PDF named clearly. Open it, check that it is readable and email it to yourself.

Skill 13: Calendar and time management

What it is. A digital calendar shows your days and lets you schedule events, set reminders and share your availability. Google Calendar and the calendar on your phone are common examples.

Why it matters. Missing a meeting or a deadline is the quickest way to lose trust. A working calendar means you stop relying on memory and start relying on a system.

What to learn.

  • How to create an event with a title, date, time and place.
  • How to set a reminder or alert, such as ten minutes before and one day before.
  • How to make an event repeat, for example a weekly study hour.
  • How to use colours for different parts of life: work, study, family, rest.
  • How to check time zones. If you work with someone in another country, a meeting at "3 pm" can mean very different things. Most calendars let you add a second time zone.
  • How to invite someone to an event and accept or decline an invitation.
  • How to block time for focused work, which means putting a "meeting with myself" in the calendar so the time is protected.

Free tool. Google Calendar or your phone's calendar.

Practise it. Create three things: a repeating weekly event for learning, a one-time appointment with a reminder, and a "focus hour" block for tomorrow. Set the alerts and make sure your phone is allowed to send notifications.

Pro Tip 💡 Put your tasks that have a time in the calendar, and your tasks that have no time in a to-do list. Mixing them is how things fall through gaps.

Skill 14: Task management

What it is. A task manager is a tool that holds your to-do list. It can be as plain as a notes list or as organised as a project board with columns. Google Tasks, Trello, Notion and Todoist are examples.

Why it matters. Your brain is for thinking, not for storing a hundred small reminders. When tasks live in one trusted place, your mind relaxes and you actually finish things.

What to learn.

  • How to write a task so it is clear. "Website" is vague. "Write the About page text" is clear.
  • How to give a task a due date and a priority.
  • How to break a big goal into small steps. "Start a business" is not a task. "Choose three business ideas" is.
  • The idea of a board with three columns: To do, Doing and Done. Moving a card across the board shows progress and feels wonderful.
  • How to review your list each morning and each week.
  • How to use a daily top three: choose three tasks that matter most today and do those first.

Free tool. Trello, Google Tasks, Notion or the simple to-do list on your phone. Check current free plans.

Practise it. Create a board with three columns. Write five tasks from your week, one per card. Move one card to Done today.

Skill 15: Note-taking

What it is. Capturing ideas, facts and plans in a place where you can find them again. Notes can be typed, handwritten and photographed, or even spoken as voice notes.

Why it matters. Information you do not record is information you lose. Good notes feed your studying, your writing and your decisions.

What to learn.

  • How to create a note, give it a title and organise notes into folders or with tags.
  • How to use bullets and headings inside a note.
  • How to make a checklist inside a note.
  • How to search across all your notes.
  • How to capture quickly: voice notes while walking, a photo of a whiteboard, a screenshot of something useful.
  • A simple habit: after learning anything, write three lines in your own words. That alone doubles how much you remember.

Free tool. The notes app on your phone, Google Keep, Notion or OneNote.

Practise it. Create a note titled "Things I want to learn." Add five items with a checkbox beside each. Add a voice note describing one thing you learned today. Then search for the word "learn" to make sure you can find it again.

8Area Four: Communicating And Collaborating Online (Skills 16 To 18)

Working online is mostly about working with other people through screens. These three skills are the difference between being someone who does good work and being someone people love to work with.

Skill 16: Video calls

What it is. A video call lets you see and hear people live over the internet. Zoom, Google Meet and Microsoft Teams are the best known.

Why it matters. Interviews, client meetings, classes and team catch-ups now happen on video. Feeling calm and prepared on a call is a professional advantage.

What to learn.

  • How to join a call from a link, and how to start your own and send the link.
  • How to mute and unmute your microphone and turn your camera on and off.
  • How to share your screen so others can see your presentation or document.
  • How to use the chat box for links and questions.
  • How to test your audio, camera and internet before an important call.
  • Simple call manners: join a few minutes early, mute when you are not speaking, look at the camera when you talk and avoid eating loudly.
  • How to prepare your space: face a window or lamp for light, keep the background tidy, and use headphones if you can.
  • What to do when your connection drops: rejoin the link, send a short message to explain and, if needed, switch to audio only.

Free tool. Google Meet, Zoom and others have free tiers with limits. Check current time limits and features.

Practise it. Ask a friend to join a short practice call with you. Practise muting, screen sharing, using chat and leaving the call. Notice your own lighting and sound.

Pause For A Second 🌸 Nerves on camera are completely normal. Pen three sentences you can say to open any call, such as "Hello everyone, thank you for joining, I am happy to be here." Having your first line ready makes the rest easier.

Skill 17: Messaging and professional online communication

What it is. Writing short messages in chat tools such as WhatsApp, Slack, Microsoft Teams, LinkedIn or email, in a way that is clear, kind and professional.

Why it matters. When you cannot see someone's face, your words carry everything. A clear message saves time. A vague or rude one causes confusion and damages trust.

What to learn.

  • Tone. Greet first, be polite, be direct. "Hi Mr Bello, quick question about the Friday deadline" beats "Is it Friday?"
  • Clarity. Put the main point in the first line. Say what you need, from whom and by when.
  • Response time. Reply within a reasonable time, even if only to say "I have seen this and will get back to you tomorrow."
  • Boundaries. It is fine to say "I will look at this in the morning." You do not have to be available at all hours.
  • Voice notes and emojis. Fine among friends and in casual teams. In formal settings, follow the other person's lead.
  • Confidentiality. Do not share a client's private information in group chats.
  • Re-reading. If a message makes you angry, wait before replying.

A simple message formula. Greeting, context, request, deadline, thanks. Example: "Hi Tolu, thank you for the brief. I have a question about the logo size. Could you confirm whether you need it for Instagram or for print? I can finish by Thursday once I know. Thank you!"

Free tool. Whatever chat tool you or your team uses.

Practise it. Rewrite these three messages so they are clear and polite: "Where is my payment," "Send me the file," and "I can't do Tuesday." Then compare with your first versions.

Skill 18: Collaborating online

What it is. Working on the same file or project as other people at the same time or in turns, through shared documents, comments and project boards.

Why it matters. Most modern work is shared. Knowing how to share safely and give and receive feedback makes you a smooth teammate and a trusted freelancer.

What to learn.

  • How to share a document by link or by email, and how to choose the right permission. View means they can only read. Comment means they can leave notes. Edit means they can change the file.
  • How to make sure a link is not open to everyone unless you want it to be.
  • How to leave and answer comments and suggestions.
  • How to view version history, which lets you see old versions of a file and restore one if something goes wrong.
  • How to name files so everyone understands them.
  • How to say "I have made the changes, please check" clearly.
  • How to give feedback kindly: say what works, then what could improve and offer a suggestion.

Free tool. Google Docs, Sheets and Slides, plus comments and the "Share" button.

Practise it. Create a short document, share it with a friend with "Comment" permission only, ask them to leave two comments, and reply to both. Then open the version history and look at the earlier versions.

Celebrate Yourself 🎉 If you have worked through the skills so far and practised each one, you have covered more of the practical basics than most job seekers ever deliberately learn. Stop for a minute and let that be true.

9Area Five: Creating Online (Skills 19 To 22)

Now we move from using tools to making things. This area is where many women first see how these skills could become income, because creating something visible and useful is what people pay for.

Skill 19: Design basics with Canva

What it is. Graphic design means arranging pictures, text and colour so a message is clear and pleasant to look at. Canva is a free, beginner-friendly design tool that works in a browser and on a phone. It offers ready-made templates for posters, social media posts, CVs, presentations and more. Check current features and which items are free.

Why it matters. Almost every business and creator needs simple visuals. Even if you never become a designer, you can make a neat flyer, a clean CV or a branded social media post.

What to learn.

  • How to start from a template and customise it.
  • How to add and edit text, pictures and shapes.
  • How to choose two or three colours and two fonts and stick to them. Too many fonts is the quickest way to look messy.
  • The basic ideas of contrast (text stands out from the background), alignment (things line up) and white space (breathing room around elements).
  • How to resize a design for different uses, such as a post versus a story.
  • How to download your design as an image or PDF.
  • How to be careful about licences. Not every image or font can be used for every purpose, especially commercial work. Check the usage rules for any element you use.

Free tool. Canva's free plan, or another free design tool.

Practise it. Make a simple "Open to Work" or "Hello, I am Ruth" graphic. Use a template, change the text and colours, keep it to two fonts and download it.

Skill 20: Phone photo and video basics

What it is. Taking clear photos and short videos with the phone you already own, and doing simple edits such as trimming, cropping and adding captions.

Why it matters. Clear visuals build trust, whether you are posting about your work, selling a product or recording a message. You do not need an expensive camera.

What to learn.

  • Light. Natural light from a window makes almost anything look better. Avoid harsh light directly behind you.
  • Steadiness. Hold your phone with two hands or rest it on something.
  • Framing. Keep the subject in the middle or on a third of the screen and leave a little space around it. Turn on the grid lines in your camera settings to help.
  • Clean lens. Wipe it with a soft cloth. A smudged lens ruins more photos than anything.
  • Sound. For video, quiet surroundings matter more than picture quality. People forgive a plain picture but not echoey, noisy sound.
  • Simple editing. Trim the start and end of a clip, adjust brightness and crop. Your phone's built-in editor does this.
  • Captions. Many people watch with the sound off. Add captions to short videos, and check them for mistakes.
  • Consent. Ask before filming or posting other people.

Free tool. Your phone's camera and editor. CapCut and similar free apps help with video. Check current features and terms.

Practise it. Take three photos of the same object, one in dim light, one near a window and one with a tidy background. Compare them. Record a ten-second video introducing yourself and trim it.

Skill 21: Writing for the internet

What it is. Writing clear, short, scannable text for screens: emails, social captions, descriptions, bios, simple web pages.

Why it matters. People read online in a hurry. If your writing is clear, they understand and trust you. If it is confusing or too long, they leave.

What to learn.

  • Say the main thing first. Do not make people dig for it.
  • Use short sentences and short paragraphs. Two or three lines per paragraph is plenty.
  • Write the way you speak, but tidied up. Imagine you are explaining it to one friend.
  • Use headings and bullets for longer text.
  • Cut filler. Words like "very," "really" and "just" can often go.
  • Write a useful headline or subject line that says what is inside.
  • End with one clear next step. "Reply to this email," "Book a call," "Download the file."
  • Proofread. Read it aloud and check names, dates and numbers.

A simple bio formula. "I am [name], a [what you do] who helps [who] with [what result]. Based in [place]. Say hello at [contact]."

Free tool. Google Docs for drafting, plus a free spell check. You can also ask an AI tool for feedback, which we cover in Skill 24.

Practise it. Write a three-sentence bio using the formula. Then write a short caption for a post about something you learned today, and cut it by one third.

Skill 22: Social media basics

What it is. Using platforms such as Instagram, TikTok, Facebook, X, LinkedIn, Pinterest and YouTube, not only to scroll, but to set up a profile, post, interact and understand how each platform works.

Why it matters. For many jobs, businesses and freelance careers, social platforms are the shop window. Even a simple, professional presence helps people find and trust you.

What to learn.

  • How to set up a profile: a clear photo, a short bio, a link and a consistent name.
  • The difference between a personal account and a business or creator account, and what each offers. Check current options on each platform.
  • How to post, schedule, reply to comments and message people politely.
  • What each platform is mostly good for. LinkedIn is for professional connections and jobs. Instagram and TikTok are for visual and short video content. Pinterest is for ideas people search for. X is for quick public conversation. Facebook groups are for communities. YouTube is for longer videos people search for.
  • How algorithms work in simple terms: platforms show people more of what they interact with, so useful, clear and consistent content tends to travel further. Nobody outside the platform knows the exact rules, and they change.
  • How to protect your time. Decide when you use social media for work and when you switch off.
  • How to handle negative comments: mute, block or ignore, and do not argue with strangers.

Free tool. The platforms themselves, plus their built-in scheduling features. Check current availability.

Practise it. Choose one platform. Update your photo, bio and link so someone who finds you understands in five seconds what you do or are learning. Post one thing and reply to two comments or posts from others.

10Area Six: Thinking And Earning Online (Skills 23 To 25)

The last three skills are about judgment and money. They are the ones that quietly separate people who are merely comfortable online from people who can build something.

Skill 23: Research and fact-checking

What it is. Finding information online and deciding whether it is true, current and useful. Fact-checking means testing a claim before you believe it or share it.

Why it matters. The internet contains excellent information and complete nonsense, often side by side. If you cannot tell them apart, you can waste money, follow bad advice or spread false claims to others.

What to learn.

  • Who wrote this? Look for an author, an organisation and a way to contact them. A page with no author and no source deserves caution.
  • What is the evidence? A claim with a link to a study, a law or an official page is stronger than a claim with a confident tone.
  • When was it written? Old advice about prices, rules and apps is often wrong now.
  • Does anyone else say the same? Check at least two independent sources. "Independent" means they did not simply copy each other.
  • Who benefits? If a page is trying to sell you a course, a pill or a programme, remember it has a reason to make the problem sound urgent.
  • Check images. A reverse image search, available in most search engines, can show where a photo first appeared.
  • Beware emotional bait. Posts designed to make you furious or terrified are often designed to be shared, not to be true.
  • Keep your sources. When you research something important, save the links in a note so you can return to them.

Free tool. A search engine, official government and organisation websites, and reputable news and reference sites.

Practise it. Pick one claim you have seen recently, such as "this app pays you to play games." Spend ten minutes looking for who says it, what evidence they give and whether independent sources agree. Write down your conclusion and your reason.

Skill 24: Using AI assistants well

What it is. An AI assistant is a program you can talk to in plain words that can explain, draft, summarise, brainstorm and answer questions. Tools such as ChatGPT, Claude and others work this way. You type a request, called a prompt, and it replies.

Why it matters. Used well, an AI assistant is like a patient tutor and a first-draft helper that is available at any hour. Used badly, it can produce confident mistakes. Knowing the difference is now a real digital skill.

What to learn.

  • Be specific in your prompt. Compare "Help me with my CV" with "I am applying for a customer service job. Here is my current CV text. Please suggest three ways to make my experience section clearer and keep it to one page."
  • Give context. Tell it who you are, who the reader is and what you want.
  • Ask it to explain. "Explain this to me like I am new to it" and "Give me an example" are wonderful prompts for learning.
  • Ask follow-ups. The first answer is a starting point. Say "make it shorter," "make it warmer" or "show me another way."
  • Check everything that matters. AI tools can state wrong facts, invent sources and sound sure about it. Verify names, numbers, dates and legal or medical claims against reliable sources.
  • Protect private information. Do not paste passwords, ID numbers, bank details or confidential client information into any tool unless you have checked its privacy rules.
  • Keep your own voice. Use the tool to help you think and draft, then rewrite in your words. Writing that sounds like everyone else does not make you stand out.
  • Be honest about use. Some schools, employers and clients have rules about AI help. Follow them.

Free tool. The free versions of the major AI assistants. Limits and features change, so check current details.

Practise it. Ask an AI assistant to explain what a spreadsheet formula is in simple words. Then ask it to create a ten-minute practice exercise. Then ask yourself: did it make any mistake? Check one fact it gave you.

Playbook Note

Private — saved only in this browser.

Skill 25: Online payments and getting paid safely

What it is. Understanding how money moves online: how to pay for things, how to receive payments, how to send an invoice and how to keep your money safe.

Why it matters. The moment your skills earn anything, you need to receive money properly and protect yourself from fake payments. This is also where scams are most costly.

What to learn.

  • The main ways money moves. Bank transfers, card payments, mobile money in some countries, and payment services such as PayPal or Wise. Which ones exist and work well depends on your country, so check what is available and legal where you live.
  • How to read the details. Fees, exchange rates and processing times can differ a lot. Always look at what you will actually receive.
  • What an invoice is. A document that tells a client what they owe, for what, by when and how to pay. It should include your name, the client's name, a date, a clear description, the amount and payment instructions.
  • How to check that a payment has really arrived. Look at your own account, not at a screenshot someone sends you. Fake payment screenshots are a common trick.
  • Beware overpayment scams. If someone "accidentally" sends too much and asks you to return the difference, do not. The original payment is often fake or will be reversed.
  • Keep records. Save invoices, receipts and payment confirmations in a folder. You will need them for budgeting and for tax.
  • Tax and legal. Rules about reporting income differ by country. I am not a tax adviser, so please check your country's rules or speak to a qualified person.
  • Open a separate account if you can. Keeping your work money apart from your personal spending makes life much easier.

Free tool. Your bank's app, a free invoice template in Google Docs or Sheets, and the payment platforms that operate in your country. Check current fees and rules.

Practise it. Create a simple invoice for a made-up job: "Social media post design, one piece, 20 dollars, due in seven days." Save it as a PDF. Do not send it to anyone, because it is only a practice. Then create a folder called "Money Records" with subfolders for invoices and receipts.

For a deeper lesson on this, read How To Get Paid As A Freelancer and Budget Like A Queen.

11How To Learn Any Digital Skill

You now have 25 skills to work on. How do you actually learn them without burning out? Here is the method, and it works for these skills and for almost any new one you will ever meet.

The learn, do, review loop

Every time you learn a skill, go through three small stages.

Learn. Watch a short tutorial or read a short explanation. Keep it to ten or fifteen minutes. Do not binge ten videos in a row, because you will remember almost none of them.

Do. Immediately practise what you just learned, on your own device, without the video playing. This is where learning actually happens.

Review. Tomorrow, repeat the task from memory. If you can do it, tick it on your skills map. If you cannot, watch the part you missed and try again.

The gap between "I watched it" and "I can do it" is where most people give up. Do not skip the middle step.

Copy first, create later

When you are new, copy examples. Follow a tutorial exactly. Rebuild a template. Retype a well-written email in your own words. Copying is not cheating. It is how every craftsperson learns. Creativity comes after you understand the basics.

Where to learn for free

  • Official help centres. Almost every tool has a free guide written by the people who made it.
  • Video platforms. Search for "[tool name] for beginners" and choose a short, recent video. Check the date, because interfaces change.
  • Free courses. Our own free Academy on this site has beginner-friendly courses. Other sites and libraries offer free options too.
  • Library and community centres. Many offer free computer access and sometimes classes.
  • Friends and groups. A friend who is slightly ahead of you is often the best teacher. Online communities can help too, but treat advice from strangers with care.

How to judge a tutorial quickly

Before you spend twenty minutes on a video, check: Is it recent? Does it start with the result you want? Does the person show their screen clearly? Do the comments say it worked? If the answer to most is yes, begin. If not, try another.

How to get unstuck without quitting

When you hit a wall, do these in order. First, take a short break and breathe. Second, read the error message slowly, because it often tells you the problem. Third, search for the exact words of the problem. Fourth, ask a friend or a community. Fifth, leave it for a day and return. Being stuck is not a sign you are bad at this. It is a normal part of learning.

Set up a learning rhythm

Pick a time you can keep. Twenty focused minutes a day beats a three-hour Sunday burst. Put the time in your calendar. Keep your phone's distractions away while you practise. And on the days you miss, simply begin again the next day without drama.

Big Sis Note 💖 Please do not compare your day three with someone else's year three. The women who look effortless online practised a great deal where nobody could see.

12Putting The 25 Skills Together

Skills become powerful when they work together. Here are a few small examples of how they combine, each made up to show the idea.

Making a CV that gets read. Skill 9 (documents) to write it. Skill 21 (writing) to keep it clear. Skill 19 (design) to make it neat. Skill 12 (PDF) to export it. Skill 4 (email) to send it with a good subject line. Skill 5 (files) to name it properly. That is six skills in one small task.

Booking and running an online meeting. Skill 13 (calendar) to schedule. Skill 4 (email) to invite. Skill 16 (video calls) to host. Skill 11 (slides) to present. Skill 18 (collaboration) to share notes. Skill 14 (tasks) to track the follow-ups.

Starting a tiny side business. Skill 22 (social media) and Skill 19 (design) to show your work. Skill 20 (photo and video) to capture it. Skill 25 (payments) to get paid. Skill 10 (spreadsheets) to track money. Skills 6, 7 and 8 to stay safe through all of it.

Notice how none of these are mysterious. They are small abilities joined together. That is why strong foundations matter so much.

13Where To Go: Finding Opportunities With Your Skills

Skills are the engine, but you still need a road. This chapter shows you where to look for real work, practice and connections. You do not need all of these places. Choose two or three and show up there consistently.

Your warm network (start here)

Your warm network means people who already know you: friends, family, former classmates, neighbours, teachers, colleagues, people from your church or community groups. These are your safest first stop. Many first opportunities, such as small tasks, referrals and introductions, come from someone who simply knows you are capable.

A simple message might be: "Hi Chioma, I am building my digital skills and I am looking for small tasks to practise on, like tidying a document, making a simple flyer or organising a spreadsheet. If you know anyone who could use a hand, I would really appreciate an introduction."

LinkedIn

LinkedIn is a professional network. Create a profile with a clear photo, a headline that says what you do or are learning, and a short "About" section. Connect with people you know, follow companies you admire and comment thoughtfully on posts. Many employers and recruiters search here. Be polite and specific when you message people, and never pay anyone who promises you a job.

X (formerly Twitter)

X is a fast, public platform. Useful for following people in your field, joining conversations and sharing short lessons. Keep your account professional if you plan to be found by clients or employers.

Facebook groups

Search for groups about your interest or location, such as remote work, a skill or your city. Read the rules first. Be helpful before you promote yourself. Avoid groups where members push "get rich quick" offers.

Instagram

Good for visual work and personal brands. Share short examples of what you can do, such as a tidy flyer or a simple before-and-after. Use a clear bio and send polite messages to small businesses you could help.

TikTok

Short videos can introduce you to people you would never otherwise meet. Share short lessons, simple demonstrations or your learning journey, if you are comfortable on camera, or show only your screen and hands if you are not. Check current platform rules and avoid anything that promises unrealistic income.

Pinterest

People use Pinterest to search for ideas. If you can design, write or organise, pins that link to useful content can bring steady visitors over time. It tends to reward patience.

Reddit

Reddit has communities for almost every topic. Read each community's rules, because many ban self-promotion. Ask honest questions, answer others when you can, and never spam.

Marketplaces and job boards

Freelance marketplaces and remote job boards list small and large jobs. Create a clear profile, and apply with a short, personal message that responds to the exact request. Read the platform's rules and fees, and never take payment or conversations off the platform if the rules forbid it. Be wary of any job that asks you to pay first.

Local and in-person

Do not forget your own town. Small businesses, schools, clinics, shops and churches often need help with posters, forms, social pages and spreadsheets. A short, friendly visit or a phone call can start a real conversation.

How to choose your two or three

Ask yourself: where do the people I want to help already spend time? Where am I comfortable showing up weekly? Pick your warm network plus one or two other places and stay with them for at least a month before deciding if they work.

14Cold Email, Message And Call Scripts

A cold message is a message to someone who does not know you yet. It sounds scary, but it is just a polite, short introduction. Here is how to do it kindly and well.

The kind and legal way to contact people

Be respectful. Send a personal message, not a copy-paste blast to hundreds of people. Say who you are and why you are writing. Make it easy to say no, and if someone says "no thank you" or "please stop," stop immediately. Rules about unsolicited emails, text messages and phone calls differ by country and sometimes by industry, so please check your local rules before contacting strangers. If you are unsure, stick to your warm network and to businesses that have published a contact address for enquiries.

The anatomy of a good cold message

A good first message has five small parts: a greeting, a reason you are writing to this person specifically, one clear offer or question, proof or context in one line, and an easy next step.

Keep it under about 100 words. Nobody reads long messages from strangers.

Script one: a short email to a small business

Subject: A quick idea for your Instagram page

"Hello Mrs Adebayo,

I came across your bakery page and loved the cake photos. I noticed the last post was a few weeks ago, and I thought you might like some help keeping it active.

I am learning social media management and I would love to create three simple, ready-to-post designs for you as a small trial, free of charge, so you can see if it is useful.

Would you be open to that? If not, no problem at all, and thank you for reading.

Warm regards, Ruth Eze"

(Please note that this is a made-up example. Replace every detail with your own.)

Script two: a short direct message on Instagram or LinkedIn

"Hi Tunde, I really enjoyed your recent post about starting a tailoring business. I am practising spreadsheet skills and I am looking for one small project to help with, such as a price list or an order tracker. Would you be open to me making a simple sample for you to look at? No pressure at all."

Script three: a follow-up message

Send this once, about five to seven days after the first message, if you have heard nothing.

"Hi Mrs Adebayo, I just wanted to follow up on my note from last week in case it got buried. No worries if the timing is not right. Thank you again for your time."

If you still hear nothing, let it go gracefully. Do not message a third and fourth time.

Script four: replying when someone is interested

"Thank you so much for getting back to me! To make sure I do this properly, could you tell me what you would like, by when, and where I should send it? I will confirm everything in a short message so we are both clear."

Script five: replying when someone says no

"Thank you for letting me know, and thank you for your time. If anything changes, I would be glad to help. Have a lovely week."

A kind reply to a "no" sometimes leads to a "yes" later or to a recommendation.

Script six: a short phone call

Use this only where phone contact is appropriate and legal, and think carefully about the person's time.

"Hello, this is Ruth. Is this a good moment for a quick question? I help small businesses with simple design and organisation, and I am looking for a first project to practise on. I saw that your shop does not have a price list posted online. Would it be helpful if I made a simple sample for you to look at?"

If they are busy, ask when would be better and say thank you.

Handling objections

"I do not have a budget." Reply: "That is completely fine. I am offering a small free sample so you can see whether it helps."

"I do not know you." Reply: "That is fair. I am happy to show you a few practice pieces so you can see my work."

"We already have someone." Reply: "That is great. If you ever need extra help, I would be glad to hear from you."

Tracking your outreach

Open a spreadsheet with these columns: name, where you found them, date contacted, what you said, reply, follow-up date and result. This one habit turns a stressful task into a calm routine and uses Skill 10 beautifully.

15A Complete Plan To Turn Your Skills Into Income

I will say this clearly: there is no guaranteed income here. But there are honest, practical ways your skills can lead to money, and here is the full picture, from the most direct to the most ambitious.

Path one: get a job that needs these skills

Many entry-level roles, such as administrative assistant, receptionist, customer support, data entry clerk, office assistant and junior operations roles, ask for exactly the skills in this guide. Your job is to show them. Update your CV with a skills section, practise a short answer to "tell me about your computer skills," and apply to roles that match. Never pay a fee to apply for a job.

Path two: freelance with a simple service

A freelancer works for different clients on separate projects instead of one employer. Beginner-friendly services that grow directly from this guide include: document formatting and CV design, spreadsheet setup and clean-up, Canva design for small businesses, social media scheduling, email inbox organisation, simple online research, and basic virtual assistance. For more, see 21 Online Skills That Can Change Your Income and How To Get Your First Freelance Client.

Path three: help people in your community learn

If you can set up an email, make a video call or scan a document, there are people around you who cannot. Offering patient, friendly tutoring to older relatives, small shop owners or neighbours can be a gentle first service. Be clear that you are teaching practical basics, set a fair price and never ask for their passwords.

Path four: build a small digital product

Once you are confident, you can turn what you know into something reusable: a spreadsheet template, a Canva template pack, a printable planner or a simple guide. See How To Create And Sell A Digital Product.

Path five: combine your skills into a small business

Over time, you may combine skills into a business, such as an admin support service for small shops, a content service for local brands or a template shop. That takes longer, and the honest advice is to start with paths one to three first.

A gentle starting price

Pricing depends on your country, your skill and your clients, so please research what is fair near you. A simple way to begin: choose one small, clearly defined package, such as "organise your inbox and set up folders" or "three social media designs." Estimate how long it takes you, decide a fair hourly value for your time and offer a small, clear price. Put your price in writing before you start. As your confidence and results grow, raise your price. Try the free Freelance Rate Calculator to think it through.

Keep it written and simple

Before any paid work, confirm in a short message: what you will deliver, by when, the price, how many changes are included and how you will be paid. For larger projects, use a simple written agreement. I am not a lawyer, so for contracts that really matter, please ask a qualified person or check your local rules.

16Tools And Setup: What You Need And What You Can Skip

You do not need a long shopping list. Here is a sensible starter setup.

The free starter kit

NeedFree option to start with
EmailGmail or Outlook
Documents, spreadsheets, slidesGoogle Docs, Sheets and Slides
Cloud storageGoogle Drive
DesignCanva free plan
Video callsGoogle Meet or Zoom free tier
Notes and tasksGoogle Keep, Trello or Notion
Password safetyYour phone's built-in password manager
PDF and scanningYour phone's scanner and free PDF tools
Practice typingA free typing website
LearningOur free Academy courses, help centres and video tutorials

Free plans and limits change, so check current details on each service.

When to pay for a tool

Only pay when a free tool is truly blocking your work, and when you are earning or confident you will use it. A paid tool does not make you skilled. Use free versions until the limit genuinely hurts.

Organise your digital life

Take one hour this week to do the following. Create your main folders. Delete apps you do not use. Unsubscribe from newsletters you never read. Make a single folder for important documents. Write your master password somewhere safe offline. Back up your phone. That one hour pays you back for years.

Protect your phone and data

Use a screen lock, such as a PIN or fingerprint. Turn on "Find my device." Keep your software updated. Install apps only from the official store. Be careful with public charging stations and public Wi-Fi. If your phone is lost, you will be glad you did these things.

17Common Mistakes (And How To Dodge Them)

Everyone makes these. Seeing them in advance saves you a lot of trouble.

Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake one is learning everything at once. Pick one skill and finish its practice before you start the next.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake two is watching without doing. Tutorials feel productive. They are not, unless you close the video and try it yourself.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake three is reusing passwords. One leaked password then opens many doors.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake four is clicking fast. Scammers depend on speed. Slow down whenever money, passwords or urgency are involved.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake five is keeping files in chaos. Name things clearly and keep a simple folder structure.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake six is never backing up. Keep important files in at least two places.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake seven is trusting every answer an AI tool or website gives. Verify anything important.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake eight is waiting until you feel ready to show your work. You become ready by sharing small pieces.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake nine is comparing yourself with experts. Compare yourself with who you were last month.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake ten is paying for expensive courses before trying free ones. Most basics are available free.

18When Things Do Not Go To Plan: A Troubleshooting Table

What is happeningWhat it usually meansWhat to try
"I watch tutorials but cannot do the task alone"You are watching more than doingClose the video, repeat the task from memory, check your notes only if stuck
"I forget what I learned"No reviewReview the next day, write three lines in your own words
"I feel overwhelmed by the list"Too many skills at onceChoose one skill this week. Ignore the rest for now
"My phone keeps running out of space"Photos, videos and appsBack up photos to the cloud, delete unused apps, clear downloads
"I cannot find my files"No folder systemCreate four main folders and move things in, ten minutes at a time
"I got a suspicious message"Possible phishingDo not click, check through the official app or site, report and delete
"I forgot my password"No recovery set upUse the "forgot password" option, then add recovery details and a password manager
"Video calls make me anxious"Normal nervesPrepare your opening line, test your setup, practise with a friend
"My messages get no reply"Too long or unclearShorten, put the request first, add a deadline and be polite
"I do not have a laptop"Limited equipmentUse your phone, a library or community centre, or a friend's device for bigger tasks
"I have no confidence to apply"Fear of being judgedApply for small, low-pressure things first and collect a few wins
"An app is asking for payment"Free trial or paid planRead what you are agreeing to, set a calendar reminder to cancel and check fees

19Scam And Safety Warnings

I will not frighten you, but I will be honest. The moment you start looking for work and money online, scammers notice. Here is what to watch for.

Common scams aimed at beginners

  • Fake job offers. Messages offering high pay for very little work, often through chat apps, with no interview.
  • Advance fee scams. Anyone who asks you to pay to get a job, to "release" money or to unlock a prize.
  • Fake cheque and overpayment scams. A client sends too much and asks for a refund before the original payment clears.
  • Task and "like and earn" scams. You are asked to complete small tasks, then told to deposit your own money to continue.
  • Fake courses and "guaranteed income" programmes. High-pressure sales, income screenshots and promises that sound too good.
  • Impersonation. Someone pretending to be a recruiter, a bank, a delivery company or a friend.
  • Fake websites and login pages. A page copied to look like a real one so it can steal your password.
  • Romance and friendship scams. A new online "friend" who eventually asks for money.

Safety habits

Slow down. Verify through another channel. Never share verification codes, PINs or full passwords. Do not pay to start work. Keep communication and payments on the official platform. Research a company before you share personal documents. Trust the awkward feeling in your stomach.

If you think you have been scammed

First, do not panic and do not blame yourself. Second, stop contact with the scammer. Third, if you shared a password, change it immediately, starting with your email, and turn on two-step verification. Fourth, contact your bank or payment provider right away, because quick action can sometimes help. Fifth, save screenshots, messages and payment details as evidence. Sixth, report it to the platform and to the appropriate authority in your country. Finally, tell someone you trust. Scammers rely on shame. You do not owe them your silence.

20Your First Seven Days: A Gentle Quick Start

If you would like to begin right now without thinking about it, follow this simple week. Each day takes about twenty to thirty minutes.

Day 1. Do the self-check. Write your three most urgent skills at the top of your skills map.

Day 2. Secure your email. Create a long new password, turn on two-step verification and set a recovery option.

Day 3. Set up your folders. Create your main folders and upload your important documents to cloud storage with clear names.

Day 4. Practise safety. Look through your spam folder, find the warning signs in three messages and review the privacy settings on one social account.

Day 5. Make something. Write a one-page "About Me" document and download it as a PDF. Make one Canva graphic.

Day 6. Organise your time. Set up your calendar with a weekly learning block and create a three-column task board.

Day 7. Review. Look at your skills map. Tick what you can do from memory. Choose the next three skills to practise. Celebrate what you finished.

21Your Thirty-Day Plan

Once your first week is done, here is a gentle thirty-day plan that covers all 25 skills with room to breathe. Each day is about twenty to thirty minutes. If you miss a day, pick up where you stopped. There is no penalty.

Week one: safe and organised

  • Days 1 to 2: Skills 1 and 2. Tidy your phone settings and learn the key shortcuts.
  • Day 3: Skill 3. Practise searching and bookmarking.
  • Day 4: Skill 4. Create a professional email signature and send yourself a test email.
  • Day 5: Skill 5. Build your folder system and back up your important documents.
  • Day 6: Skills 6 and 7. Strengthen your passwords and study three scam messages.
  • Day 7: Skill 8. Review privacy settings and do a self-search.

Week two: everyday productivity

  • Day 8: Skill 9. Write and format a one-page document.
  • Day 9: Skill 10. Build a small budget spreadsheet.
  • Day 10: Skill 11. Make a five-slide presentation.
  • Day 11: Skill 12. Scan a paper document and sign a PDF.
  • Day 12: Skill 13. Set up your calendar with reminders.
  • Day 13: Skill 14. Create a task board.
  • Day 14: Skill 15. Build a note system and review the week.

Week three: communicating and creating

  • Day 15: Skill 16. Do a practice video call.
  • Day 16: Skill 17. Rewrite three messages in a clear, polite way.
  • Day 17: Skill 18. Share a document and practise comments.
  • Day 18: Skill 19. Make two Canva designs.
  • Day 19: Skill 20. Take photos in good light and trim a short video.
  • Day 20: Skill 21. Write your bio and a short caption.
  • Day 21: Skill 22. Update one social profile and make one post.

Week four: judgment, money and your next step

  • Day 22: Skill 23. Fact-check one claim.
  • Day 23: Skill 24. Practise three good prompts and verify the answers.
  • Day 24: Skill 25. Create a practice invoice and a money records folder.
  • Day 25: Combine skills. Make a polished CV using documents, writing, design and PDF export.
  • Day 26: Write your one-line offer: "I help [who] with [what]."
  • Day 27: Make your list of twenty people in your warm network and local area.
  • Day 28: Send your first five messages using the scripts.
  • Day 29: Follow up and track replies.
  • Day 30: Review your skills map and write your next thirty-day goal.

22Your Ninety-Day Plan

If you want to go further, here is a simple structure for three months.

Days 1 to 30: learn and organise

Complete the thirty-day plan. By day thirty you should have a safe email, tidy files, a skills map with most skills ticked and a few pieces of practice work.

Days 31 to 60: build proof and reach out

Choose one direction: a job, a freelance service or helping people locally. Build three to five pieces of practice work that match it, such as a clean CV, a Canva set, a spreadsheet template or a tidy document. Put them in one online folder or a simple profile. Send messages to twenty to thirty people or businesses, polite and personal. Take one free course in the Academy that fits your direction.

Days 61 to 90: earn and refine

Apply for suitable jobs or offer your first small paid package. Ask for honest feedback. Ask for a short testimonial from anyone you helped, and only share it with permission. Improve your weakest skill. Raise your price a little if people say yes quickly. Write your next ninety-day goal.

At the end, do a short review. What worked? What did I enjoy? What drained me? What will I do more of? What will I drop?

23Working With A Real Client Or Employer: What Happens After "Yes"

Many beginners panic when someone finally says yes. Here is a calm walk-through.

Confirm the details in writing. Send a short message that repeats what was agreed: what you will do, when you will deliver, the price and how you will be paid.

Do the work in small, visible steps. For bigger tasks, send a quick draft before you finish. It prevents big surprises.

Deliver neatly. Name your files clearly. Send everything in one message, with a short note explaining what is attached and what the next step is.

Handle feedback calmly. Feedback is about the work, not about you. Say "Thank you, I will update that," then do it.

Ask for a testimonial and a referral. After a good result, politely ask whether they would write a line about your work and whether they know anyone else who might need help.

Keep records. Save the agreement, the files and the payment confirmation in a clearly named folder.

Be honest. If you do not know how to do something, say so and learn it. Do not pretend. Clients forgive a learner, but they do not forgive a bluff.

24A Weekly Rhythm After The First Month

When the plan ends, a simple weekly rhythm keeps you growing without exhaustion.

  • Practise (three sessions of twenty minutes). Pick a skill that needs strengthening.
  • Make (one session). Create something real, such as a design, a spreadsheet template or a short piece of writing.
  • Reach out (one session). Send a few polite messages or applications.
  • Tidy (ten minutes). Clear your inbox, file your documents and update your task board.
  • Review (ten minutes on Sunday). Look at your week and choose three priorities for the next one.

Tracking your money simply

Once any money comes in, keep a tiny spreadsheet: date, who paid, what for, amount and when it arrived. Do it on the day. It protects you at tax time and shows what is working. For a full lesson, read Budget Like A Queen.

25Mindset: The Voices That Show Up

When you learn new things, certain voices appear. Here is how to answer them.

"I am too old / too late." Many of the people learning these skills are adults who started in their thirties, forties and beyond. The best time to start is the day you decide to.

"I am not a tech person." Neither are most people who are good with technology. They are simply people who practised.

"Everyone else already knows this." They do not. They just talk less about what they do not know.

"I will make a mistake." You will. Mistakes in a practice file cost nothing. In fact, they are the lesson.

"What if I fail?" Then you will know what to adjust. That is not failure. That is information.

You are not behind. You are beginning.

26Questions Girls Ask Me

Can I learn these skills with only a phone?

Yes, many of them. Email, files, calendar, notes, Canva, video calls, photo and video, social media and AI tools all work on a phone. A computer makes documents, spreadsheets and long typing easier, so borrow one occasionally, for example at a library or community centre, when you need it.

How long does it take to learn all 25 skills?

Most people can reach a comfortable beginner level in one to three months with about twenty minutes a day. Mastery takes longer and is never fully finished, because tools keep changing. You are aiming for confidence, not perfection.

Which skill should I start with?

Start with the safety skills (6, 7 and 8) and email (4), because they protect you and unlock everything else. After that, go in the order that suits your goals.

Do I need to pay for courses?

No. Everything in this guide can be learned with free tools. Paid courses can help, but only choose one after you have tried free options and know what you need. Be careful of anyone promising guaranteed income.

Will these skills get me a job?

They make you more employable and more capable, but I cannot promise a job. Combine them with a clear direction, a tidy CV and steady applications. The job market varies by country and time.

Can I earn money with these skills?

Many people do, through jobs, freelancing or small services. Results vary widely and depend on your effort, your market, your pricing and your timing. Please do not believe anyone who promises guaranteed income.

How do I know whether a website or message is a scam?

Look for urgency, requests for secrets, payment demands and strange addresses. Pause, do not click, and check through the official app or by typing the address yourself. When in doubt, ask a trusted person.

Is it safe to use AI tools?

They are useful, but they can make mistakes and they do not keep your secrets by default. Do not paste passwords or private documents, check important facts, and follow the privacy rules of the tool and of any school or employer you work with.

What if I am scared of breaking something?

You almost never will. Practise on copies and test files, and remember that most tools have an undo button and a version history. Learning is much cheaper than you fear.

How do I stay motivated?

Make it small, put it in your calendar and tick off what you finish. Tell one friend what you are learning. And remember why you started.

What if I am much slower than other people?

Speed is not the point. Steady practice is. Everyone learns at a different pace, and slow learners who keep going often end up the most thorough.

What should I do after I finish this guide?

Choose a direction: a job, freelancing or a small business. Then read the guides linked below, take a free Academy course that matches it and begin reaching out.

28What To Do Next

You have reached the end of a long guide, and that tells me something lovely about you: you take your future seriously.

Here is what I want you to carry with you. Digital skills are not a talent that some women are born with. They are a set of small, learnable habits: how you protect your accounts, how you organise your files, how you write a message, how you check a claim. Anyone who practises them becomes more capable, more confident and harder to fool.

So here is your next step, and it is small. Tonight, secure your email. Tomorrow, set up your folders. This week, work through the first seven days. In a month, look back and notice how different these screens feel.

When it feels slow, remember that slow is still moving. When a tool confuses you, remember that you can always search it, ask someone or try again tomorrow. When you doubt yourself, open your skills map and look at what you can already do.

When you are ready to go further, here are good next reads. 30-Day Digital Skills Challenge takes one skill and builds it into a portfolio. I am rooting for you, babe. Begin tonight, go slowly and keep going.
